task.goal: Help a repair shop give accurate pickup estimates when parts arrival varies.
hard_constraints: Two staff, paper job cards and an existing supplier email inbox; no paid software.
Do not promise a date unsupported by parts status or hide delays.
Compare missed estimates, customer calls and staff time for four weeks.
task.available_resources: Past 30 job records and supplier replies.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Parts-status gates with a firm next-update commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace a single pickup date with explicit evidence gates on each paper job card: ordered with no confirmed dispatch; dispatched with supplier arrival range; physically received and checked; repair scheduled. The mechanism is to prevent uncertain supply information from becoming a customer promise while giving customers a reliable time to hear next.

One staff member checks supplier email at two fixed times daily and records the latest status, its timestamp and the next check on affected cards. The other uses that entry when speaking to customers; both can cover either role. Before receipt, say, for example: “The supplier reports arrival Tuesday–Thursday. Pickup is still unconfirmed; we will update you Wednesday afternoon.” Offer a conditional pickup window only when supplier evidence and available repair capacity support it, stating those conditions. Once the correct parts are received and checked, assign a pickup window against the shop’s actual workload. Notify customers promptly when evidence invalidates a previously communicated window, explaining the cause and revised status.

Use the 30 past records to identify common unsupported promises and estimate ordinary repair time after parts receipt. Implementation requires only a handwritten status key, job-card fields, the existing inbox and a daily callback list. It assumes staff can reliably connect supplier replies to jobs and reserve realistic workshop capacity. It cannot make unreliable supplier information accurate; its benefit may primarily be fewer premature promises and fewer uncertainty-driven calls. Customers needing a date immediately may find the process less satisfying.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run for four weeks, alternating new eligible jobs between this process and current practice, with both groups receiving honest delay disclosures. Use the past 30 records as context where timestamps exist, not as a complete baseline by assumption. On paper, tally missed communicated pickup dates/windows, inbound status calls and staff minutes for checks, updates and calls; record how many jobs received any pickup estimate and how early. Inspect unresolved jobs at week four separately. The mechanism is challenged if supported estimates still miss as often, calls do not fall, or communication time rises without improved reliability. Check that apparent gains are not solely due to withholding every estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Evidence-based conditional ranges from comparable past jobs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shop’s own supply history to express uncertainty as a conditional range rather than treating a supplier’s expected arrival as a certain pickup date. The mechanism is calibration: estimates reflect observed variation for comparable parts orders and include the shop’s remaining repair workload.

Review the 30 job records alongside supplier replies. Where dates are available, write down order, dispatch, receipt and ready-for-pickup dates. Group only genuinely comparable jobs, such as the same supplier and stock status; avoid creating many tiny categories. On a paper reference sheet, show the observed delivery span and the number of examples behind it. Do not describe that span as a guaranteed bound or a statistically established confidence interval. Sparse or inconsistent groups receive “insufficient evidence for a pickup window.”

For each new job, record the supplier’s current evidence and use relevant historical variation as a reasonableness check. Give a conditional pickup range only if the current supplier status, comparable history and workshop capacity support one: “If the dispatched part arrives within the supplier’s range, we expect collection Thursday–Monday; this remains provisional until it arrives.” If supplier evidence conflicts with history, investigate and explain the uncertainty rather than averaging it away. Review affected cards daily and contact customers when the range changes or becomes unsupported. Confirm pickup after parts inspection and scheduling.

One staff member maintains the reference sheet and inbox annotations; the other records communicated ranges and revisions on job cards. This needs no software beyond the inbox. It assumes useful dates and some comparable past jobs exist. Thirty records may be too few, and changing supplier conditions can invalidate historical patterns. In those cases, communicate status and the next update time instead of inventing precision.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible jobs between these conditional ranges and the shop’s current honest estimating practice. Log initial and revised windows, misses against the initial window, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Track window width, lead time and jobs without estimates so broad or late ranges cannot masquerade as better accuracy. Use the historical sheet only where supporting examples are visible. A small falsifying check is whether comparable deliveries immediately fall outside its observed span repeatedly; suspend that grouping if so. Judge the process unsuccessful if misses remain comparable while windows become substantially less useful or staff time increases.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Exception-triggered supplier clarification and delay recovery
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make pickup estimates more accurate by resolving missing or contradictory parts information before it contaminates the estimate. The primary mechanism is targeted exception handling: staff pursue the few supply uncertainties threatening customer commitments instead of treating all supplier replies as equally informative.

Use the 30 past jobs and supplier replies to identify recurring warning signs, such as an order acknowledgement mistaken for dispatch, a backorder without a replenishment date, or an expected arrival passing without tracking movement. These are investigation triggers, not proof that a delivery will fail. On each paper job card, record the current supplier evidence, any supported conditional pickup window, the next supply milestone and the latest time that milestone can occur without undermining that window. Include repair time and workshop capacity when setting that threshold.

At one daily inbox review, one staff member pulls cards whose milestone is missing, overdue or contradictory. Using the existing supplier email channel, ask a specific question: Is this allocated stock? Has it dispatched? What arrival range is currently supported? Request a tracking reference where applicable. If a supported alternative part or delivery option is available, assess compatibility, cost and customer authorization before changing the order; the process does not depend on alternatives existing. The second staff member contacts affected customers as soon as their current window loses support, even if the supplier has not replied. State what changed, what is unknown and when the next update will come. Never retain an invalid window while awaiting clarification.

Implementation needs a handwritten exception list, short email templates and clear daily ownership. It assumes suppliers sometimes provide useful clarification and staff can identify milestone dependencies. Supplier silence, missing records or universal backorders may leave accuracy unchanged; escalation still cannot justify an unsupported date.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Trial for four weeks, alternating new jobs between exception handling and current practice, with equal requirements to disclose known delays. Compare missed initial pickup estimates, inbound customer status calls and staff minutes, including supplier chasing. Record estimate availability, revisions and unresolved jobs. For each trigger, note whether clarification arrived before the threatened window and whether it materially changed the estimate or repair plan. The mechanism is weakened if chasing mostly produces no actionable information, warnings arrive too late, or misses and calls remain unchanged while staff time rises. Inspect several triggered cards against their emails to verify that revised promises have actual evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A protected repair slot for jobs released by arriving parts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce pickup uncertainty by protecting workshop capacity for jobs whose parts arrive unexpectedly. The mechanism is operational: shorten and stabilize the wait between parts receipt and repair completion, so variable deliveries do not also create an unpredictable workshop queue.

Review the 30 past job cards and supplier replies for any recorded gap between parts receipt and repair start. If that gap is substantial, trial one small, protected repair block on working days. Size it using documented repair durations and the two staff members’ available hours; do not assume historical timestamps exist. Fill the rest of the schedule normally. Until a stated daily cutoff, keep the protected block available for the oldest waiting job whose complete, correct parts have arrived and whose remaining work fits. If none qualifies, release it to ordinary work. Longer repairs require separately available capacity.

Use a paper diary alongside the job cards. One staff member checks arrivals and records remaining work; the other assigns the block and communicates the resulting pickup estimate. Both can cover either role. Before parts arrive, explain that pickup remains unconfirmed and give a next-update time. After receipt and inspection, estimate pickup from an actual available block and a credible repair duration. Record and disclose delays immediately if diagnosis changes or the block becomes unavailable.

This requires no purchased tools, but it consumes scheduling flexibility and may delay other work. It assumes staff control the schedule, enough repairs fit the block, and waiting after receipt is a meaningful source of error. It will offer little benefit where supplier transit dominates the entire delay or every repair requires lengthy, unpredictable work.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two weeks of current scheduling with two weeks using protected blocks, keeping truthful status updates throughout. On paper, record missed original pickup estimates, inbound status calls and staff minutes spent scheduling, checking and communicating. Also record receipt-to-start time, completed jobs, unused block minutes and estimate availability. Report unfinished jobs separately. Inspect the first five eligible arrivals: if the protected block seldom advances their start, the mechanism lacks support. Four-week differences remain tentative because job mix and deliveries may change; reject the approach if it merely transfers delays to other customers without improving estimate reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check the whole repair requirement before estimating pickup
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce estimate failures caused by discovering an additional required part after the initially ordered part arrives. The mechanism is an early completeness check: establish which parts and diagnostic dependencies must be resolved for the whole repair, then base the estimate on the slowest unresolved requirement. This could help when individually accurate supplier arrival information still produces inaccurate pickup estimates because the original parts list was incomplete.

Review the 30 past job records and supplier replies for documented additional orders, incompatible parts or repairs that required further diagnosis after dismantling. Use those examples to create a short handwritten checklist for recurring repair types; missing documentation is not evidence that these problems never occurred.

Before ordering, the diagnosing staff member lists required parts, compatibility details and any checks that could reveal further requirements. The second staff member briefly checks that list against the diagnosis and proposed order. Perform only practical, authorized inspections; record dependencies that cannot yet be resolved. On the paper job card, give each required item its own supplier status and mark the requirement that currently controls completion.

Explain unresolved dependencies to the customer. If an inspection must wait until the first part arrives, say that pickup cannot yet be estimated reliably and commit to an update. Offer a pickup window only when the complete repair requirements, supplier evidence and available workshop time support it. Communicate newly discovered requirements and resulting delays promptly.

This needs a checklist, a few extra job-card fields and time from both staff, using the existing inbox. It assumes incomplete diagnosis or ordering contributes to delays and that some omissions are detectable beforehand. It offers little benefit when requirements are already consistently complete or delivery variation alone causes misses.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For four weeks, alternate new eligible jobs between the completeness check and ordinary diagnosis and ordering, with both groups disclosing uncertainties and delays honestly. Record misses against the first communicated pickup window, inbound customer status calls and total staff minutes, including inspection, checking, supplier correspondence and customer updates. Also record additional orders discovered after the initial order, estimate availability and unfinished jobs.

Inspect the first five checked jobs: did the review identify a necessary item or unresolved dependency that ordinary preparation had missed? Compare subsequent additional-order delays across groups. The mechanism lacks support if checks uncover no useful omissions and additional-order delays remain similar while staff time increases. Treat four-week differences as tentative if volumes are small; do not count withholding all estimates as improved accuracy.

EXPAND.title: Reserve repair capacity behind each supported estimate
EXPAND.proposal:
Make workshop capacity a reserved resource whenever a pickup estimate is communicated. The strongest prior route—parts-status gates—depends on staff having a realistic view of capacity. Several jobs can pass its parts gate together and compete for the same repair time. This route addresses that dependency directly.

Use the 30 records to identify rough repair-duration categories where recorded work supports them. On paper, draw the next two weeks of available workshop time, subtracting existing work and routine duties. One staff member owns this sheet; the other checks it before communicating an estimate. Both use conservative judgment where duration records are weak.

At job intake, inspect the required work and supplier evidence. Give a conditional pickup window only when that evidence supports an arrival range and a specific repair slot can be provisionally reserved after it. Write the reservation and its parts-arrival cutoff on the job card. If arrival is unknown or no slot is available, communicate status and a next-update time. Do not reserve overlapping promises against the same capacity.

At each daily review, release reservations whose arrival cutoff has passed, tell affected customers immediately, and offer the next window only when supply evidence supports it. When correct parts arrive, confirm the reservation after inspection. At staff handoff, transfer the sheet and outstanding customer updates together.

This needs paper, the existing inbox and staff agreement about usable hours. It cannot fix unreliable arrival information. Reservations can also leave time idle, so uncommitted short jobs may fill gaps only when doing so cannot threaten a reserved job.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, one staff member maintains the trial tally. Alternate new eligible jobs between explicit capacity reservations and the prior parts-status-gate process with ordinary workload judgment. Both disclose delays. Compare missed initial pickup windows, inbound status calls and all estimating, scheduling and communication minutes. Also record estimate availability, lead time, idle reserved hours and delays displaced onto other jobs. Inspect the first five reservations against actual capacity. Stop allocating new trial reservations if they repeatedly double-book time or delay already committed work. No improvement is demonstrated if misses remain similar while idle time, staff time or other customers’ waits increase; report unfinished jobs separately.

EXPAND.title: Verify the complete parts requirement before placing the order
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent avoidable second waits by checking that the first order covers the whole known repair. The mechanism is error prevention: a seemingly accurate delivery estimate is useless if the arriving item is incompatible or another necessary part was never ordered.

Review the 30 job records and matching supplier replies for documented wrong items, omitted components or repeat orders. Use only observed issues and ordinary repair knowledge to make a short paper checklist; do not assume missing documentation proves an ordering error.

Before ordering, the staff member assessing the repair writes the equipment identifier, diagnosed work, required part identifiers and known dependent items on the job card. The other staff member checks the intended order against that card and available supplier descriptions. Resolve discrepancies through the existing inbox before treating an order as complete. Where disassembly or diagnosis is needed to establish requirements, tell the customer that a pickup estimate remains unavailable pending that work. Do not claim certainty about hidden faults.

After the check, place the normal order and communicate a conditional pickup window only if current supplier evidence and workshop capacity support it. On receipt, compare the contents with the verified requirement before confirming pickup timing. If a mismatch or newly discovered fault appears, record whether it arose from the order, supplier fulfillment or genuinely new information; contact the customer promptly and reset the estimate using current evidence.

One staff member owns ordering and the other owns the brief check, with the signed card providing handoff. No additional software is needed. The route assumes both can recognize relevant identifiers and dependencies. It may add unnecessary effort to simple repairs and will not reduce unpredictable transit delays.
EXPAND.experiment: Run for four weeks, alternating eligible new orders between the two-person completeness check and ordinary ordering with equally honest customer communication. The ordering owner tallies missed initial pickup estimates, inbound status calls and staff minutes, including inspection and reordering. Record wrong or missing parts, repeat orders and any delay caused by waiting for the checker. Audit five checked cards against supplier replies and received contents. Stop the extra check if it repeatedly delays order placement without identifying actionable discrepancies. The mechanism is unsupported if preventable repeat waits do not decrease and pickup reliability stays similar while staff time rises. Report jobs still awaiting parts separately.

EXPAND.title: Complete safe preparatory work while parts are in transit
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce the uncertain work remaining after delivery by completing useful diagnosis and preparation during the waiting period. The mechanism changes the repair sequence: pickup estimates become easier to support when parts arrival leaves a smaller, better-understood amount of work.

Inspect the 30 records for repair types where diagnosis, access, cleaning or another necessary step could reasonably occur before the replacement part arrives. Select only tasks staff already know how to perform safely and within the customer's existing repair authorization. Do not infer that every recorded delay could have been used productively.

At intake, the assessing staff member separates the job card into work possible now and work dependent on the part. Before starting early work, check that it will not leave equipment unsafe, consume scarce bench space needed for committed repairs, create substantial reassembly work or require additional authorization. Jobs failing that check follow the normal sequence.

Use available gaps to complete the selected preparation. Record what was actually completed, any newly discovered requirements and the remaining work. The second staff member uses that record and supplier evidence when communicating with the customer. If an arrival range and capacity support a conditional pickup window, base it on the remaining work; otherwise give status and a next-update commitment. New findings that change parts requirements or timing trigger prompt customer contact and an updated order where authorized.

When parts arrive, verify them, complete installation and necessary checks, then notify the customer when collection is supported. The card provides the handoff between staff. This requires existing tools, safe storage and some spare capacity. It cannot help repairs with no useful preparatory stage, and premature disassembly can increase storage, damage or rework risks.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible jobs between early preparation and the ordinary repair sequence, using the same honest estimating standard. The assessing staff member records missed initial pickup windows, inbound status calls and total staff time, including preparation, storage handling and reassembly. Also compare time from parts receipt to readiness and effects on other promised jobs. Inspect the first three prepared jobs for genuinely reduced remaining work. Stop early preparation immediately for unsafe storage or equipment condition, and suspend it for repair types showing repeated rework or displaced commitments. The route fails its comparison if shorter post-arrival work does not improve pickup reliability or calls, or if gains require excessive labor or longer waits elsewhere. Separate unfinished jobs at week four.

EXPAND.title: Choose the parts source by usable delivery evidence
EXPAND.proposal:
Improve the supply input itself by choosing among suppliers the shop can already use. The mechanism is source selection: when equivalent approved parts are available from more than one existing source, select the option with credible availability and acceptable total cost rather than automatically using the habitual source.

Match the 30 past jobs to supplier replies and record any observable gaps between stated availability, dispatch and actual receipt. Treat these as limited examples, not a dependable supplier ranking. One staff member owns a small paper comparison sheet; the other checks compatibility and any effect on the customer quote.

For a new order with meaningful arrival uncertainty, ask existing alternative suppliers through email whether the exact acceptable part is allocated and what dispatch and arrival information they can support. Limit the comparison to a brief initial inquiry so it does not become daily chasing. Compare like-for-like parts, freight, existing commercial terms and the cost of waiting for a reply. Choose an alternative only when compatibility is established, its delivery evidence is meaningfully better and the purchase fits existing authorization. Obtain customer approval before changing an agreed price or part specification. Never place duplicate orders merely to hedge uncertainty.

Record the chosen source and evidence on the job card, then give a conditional pickup window only if delivery information and workshop capacity support it. At handoff, the second staff member receives the order confirmation and customer-update obligation. If supply evidence deteriorates, disclose the delay promptly; change suppliers only after checking cancellation terms and avoiding duplicate liability.

This requires multiple usable suppliers and email responsiveness. Neither is established by the supplied materials. If the shop has only one viable source, this route is inapplicable. Historical examples may also reflect different parts or conditions.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible orders between this bounded source comparison and normal supplier selection, maintaining the same customer communication standard. The comparison owner records missed initial pickup estimates, inbound status calls and staff minutes, plus part and freight costs, ordering delay and cancellations. Record how often a credible alternative actually exists. Stop comparisons when waiting threatens the normal supplier's ordering cutoff, and suspend the route if additional costs or duplicate liabilities exceed existing authorization. A direct falsifying result is that alternative selection provides no better receipt or pickup reliability while increasing purchasing time or cost. Include orders with no supported pickup estimate and unresolved jobs so selective reporting cannot manufacture success.

EXPAND.title: Improved parts-status gates: expire unsupported estimates and track every revision
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: prior candidate 0, parts-status gates with a firm next-update commitment. This retains its mechanism: customer commitments advance only when parts evidence and repair capacity support them. The substantive improvement is an explicit expiry rule plus a permanent record of the original estimate, preventing stale windows from surviving supplier silence and revisions from concealing misses.

Use the 30 records and supplier replies to identify which messages actually established dispatch or arrival, and what repair time followed receipt. Missing history does not justify a delivery allowance. Add handwritten fields to each card: current evidence and timestamp, communicated pickup window, conditions, expiry trigger, next customer update, and actual ready time. Preserve previous windows when revising them.

One staff member reviews the inbox twice daily; the other owns customer updates, with both transferring outstanding actions at handoff. An acknowledgement without dispatch evidence supports a status report, not a pickup promise. A conditional window requires credible arrival information and available repair time. Record the latest arrival milestone that would still permit that window. If it passes without supporting evidence, withdraw the window and contact the customer that day, explaining the delay and committing to another update. Correct parts received and checked permit a firmer window based on remaining work; completion and checks permit a ready-for-collection notice.

This requires paper, the inbox and consistent ownership. If supplier replies cannot be matched confidently to jobs, request clarification and use status-only updates until resolved. If daily review becomes impossible, give no new provisional window and explicitly hand overdue customer contacts to the other staff member. Supplier uncertainty remains; this process controls unsupported promises rather than delivery itself.
EXPAND.experiment: Run for four weeks, alternating new jobs between the original gate process and this version; both disclose known delays promptly. The inbox owner allocates jobs in arrival order. Tally missed original and revised windows separately, jobs given no window, incoming status calls and staff minutes per job. Use historical records only as context where fields exist. Inspect five cards after week one for expired windows still being quoted. Stop issuing conditional windows in either arm if staff cannot maintain its checks. No reduction in misses or calls, or extra time without benefit, would argue against the added expiry procedure.

EXPAND.title: Close the communication loop with customer teach-back
EXPAND.proposal:
The primary mechanism is detecting and correcting a customer's mistaken understanding before it becomes their working pickup expectation. A technically qualified estimate can still fail operationally if the customer hears the supplier's arrival date as the collection date. Unlike changing wording alone, this process obtains feedback and acts on discrepancies.

Review the 30 job records and supplier replies for documented differences between supplier timing and customer commitments. Do not assume misunderstandings occurred where records are silent. Prepare a short paper conversation checklist using existing job cards.

At intake, the assessing staff member records the repair requirement, current parts evidence and remaining workshop work. Communicate a pickup window only when current parts information and capacity support it; otherwise state that pickup timing is unknown and give a next-update time. Then ask neutrally: “To check that I explained this clearly, what timing are you planning around?” Compare the answer with what the evidence supports. If the customer names an unsupported collection date, explain the distinction, correct it and check understanding again. Record the understood expectation and outstanding uncertainty on the card. This is a check on the shop's explanation, not customer consent to a delay.

The second staff member uses that record at handoff and repeats the check when a material change is communicated. Review the inbox daily; promptly disclose delays, explain which expectation has changed and give a supported replacement window or status-only update. Finish with a ready notice after repair and checks.

The process needs no software or extra staff. It assumes customers can be reached and participate briefly. If they cannot be reached, record the attempt and send an update through an existing agreed channel where available; never record understanding as confirmed. If language or accessibility needs prevent reliable teach-back, communicate the clearest supported status and mark understanding unverified. It cannot improve supplier performance or make an inaccurate technical estimate accurate.
EXPAND.experiment: For four weeks, alternate new jobs between ordinary evidence-based communication and the same process with teach-back. One staff member owns allocation and weekly tallies. Preserve every stated window; compare missed estimates, incoming status calls and staff minutes per job, alongside the number of unsupported customer expectations detected and corrected. After the first five teach-backs, inspect whether corrections were actually needed. Stop repeated checking when a customer declines or finds it burdensome, and count that outcome. Equal calls and misses with greater staff time would show no practical gain; corrected misunderstandings alone would not establish improved operational accuracy.
